learnings.title: What is the DOM?
learnings.answer:
## Document Object Model **DOM** stands for **Document Object Model** — an interface (API) for HTML and XML documents. When the browser parses an HTML document, it creates a **tree-like structure** from it — this is the DOM. It's used for interacting with and modifying the document structure, elements, and nodes. ## Example ```html Document Object Model

``` The DOM equivalent is a tree: ``` document └── html ├── head │ ├── meta │ └── title └── body └── div ├── p │ └── span ├── label └── input ``` The `document` object in JavaScript represents the DOM. It provides methods to select elements, update content, and manage events.

learnings.title: Event Propagation: Bubbling, Capturing, and the Three Phases
learnings.answer:
**Question:** explain event propagation. What are bubbling and capturing, how do they differ, and how do you implement both?

## The three phases

When you click an element, the event doesn't fire only there. It travels through the DOM in three phases:

1. **Capturing** — from `window` *down* to the target
2. **Target** — at the clicked element itself
3. **Bubbling** — from the target back *up* to `window`

```
          CAPTURING ↓            ↑ BUBBLING
          window                 window
            document               document
              body                   body
                div                    div
                  button  ←— TARGET —→  button
```

Every ancestor gets two chances to hear about the event: once on the way down, once on the way back up.

## Implementing both

The third argument to `addEventListener` chooses the phase:

```javascript
// Bubbling — the default
parent.addEventListener('click', handler);
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, false);

// Capturing
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, true);
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, { capture: true });
```

Only **ancestors** are affected by the flag. A listener on the target itself fires in the target phase regardless, in the order the listeners were registered.

## The difference in one line

Bubbling runs **innermost first**; capturing runs **outermost first**.

```javascript
document.querySelector('.outer')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('outer capture'), true);
document.querySelector('.inner')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('inner capture'), true);
document.querySelector('.inner')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('inner bubble'));
document.querySelector('.outer')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('outer bubble'));

// Clicking .inner logs:
// outer capture   ← down
// inner capture
// inner bubble    ← target, then up
// outer bubble
```

## Useful properties

| Property / method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event.target` | Where the event actually originated — **doesn't change** as it propagates |
| `event.currentTarget` | The element whose listener is running right now |
| `event.eventPhase` | `1` capturing, `2` target, `3` bubbling |
| `event.stopPropagation()` | Stop travelling further along the path |
| `event.stopImmediatePropagation()` | Also skip other listeners on this same element |
| `event.preventDefault()` | Cancel the default action; propagation continues |

The `target` vs `currentTarget` distinction is what makes [event delegation](/browser/152) possible.

## When capturing is actually useful

Bubbling is the default because it's what you want almost always. Capturing earns its place when you need to act **before** anything downstream can:

- Intercepting or blocking an event before a child's handler sees it
- Analytics that must record every click even if a child stops propagation
- A modal or overlay that swallows interaction with the page behind it

## Events that don't bubble

Not everything bubbles: `focus`, `blur`, `load`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`. Use the bubbling equivalents when you need delegation — `focusin`/`focusout` for focus, and `mouseover`/`mouseout` for hover.

## Related

- [Nested Click Handlers: Execution Order](/browser/147)
- [Event Delegation](/browser/152)
- [preventDefault vs stopPropagation](/browser/97)

learnings.title: Event Bubbling vs Capturing
Nested Click Handlers: Execution Order
learnings.answer:
**Question:** given nested elements with click handlers, what's the output when clicking the inner one? Show the order under both bubbling and capturing. *The exact markup wasn't included, so here's the canonical three-level version — the reasoning transfers to any nesting.* ## The setup ```html
``` ```javascript const ids = ['grandparent', 'parent', 'child']; ids.forEach((id) => { const el = document.getElementById(id); el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`${id} — bubble`)); el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`${id} — capture`), true); }); ``` ## The output Clicking `#child`: ``` grandparent — capture parent — capture child — capture ← target phase; registration order decides child — bubble parent — bubble grandparent — bubble ``` **Bubbling only** (drop the `true` listeners): `child`, `parent`, `grandparent` — inside out. **Capturing only**: `grandparent`, `parent`, `child` — outside in. ## The part that catches people On the **target itself**, the capture flag is ignored. Both of `#child`'s listeners fire in the target phase, in the order they were added. That's why `child — capture` prints before `child — bubble` here — not because of the phase, but because it was registered first. Swap the two `addEventListener` lines and the order swaps. ## Stopping it ```javascript document.getElementById('parent').addEventListener('click', (e) => { e.stopPropagation(); console.log('parent — bubble (stopped here)'); }); ``` Now clicking the child logs the three captures, the child's bubble, `parent — bubble`, and **nothing from grandparent**. Call `stopPropagation()` in a *capturing* listener on `#grandparent` and the event never reaches the child at all — the click appears to do nothing. That's the overlay-blocking technique, and also a classic bug when a library does it to you. `stopImmediatePropagation()` goes further: it also prevents other listeners **on the same element** from running. ## Why this is asked It tests whether you know propagation is a *round trip* rather than a single upward pass, and whether you understand that `target` stays fixed while `currentTarget` changes. Both are load-bearing for [delegation](/browser/152). ## Related - [Event Propagation: Bubbling, Capturing, and the Three Phases](/browser/146) - [Event Delegation](/browser/152) - [Event Bubbling vs Capturing](/browser/28)

learnings.title: event.preventDefault() vs event.stopPropagation()
learnings.answer:
## `event.preventDefault()`

Prevents the **default browser behavior** of an element:

- On a `<form>` — prevents submission
- On an `<a>` — prevents navigation
- On `contextmenu` — prevents the context menu

## `event.stopPropagation()`

Stops the event from propagating through the DOM — prevents it from firing in the **bubbling** or **capturing** phase on parent elements.

## Checking if preventDefault was called

Use `event.defaultPrevented` — returns `true` if `preventDefault()` was called on the element:

```javascript
element.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  console.log(e.defaultPrevented); // true
});
```

learnings.answer:
**Question:** given a `

A click on an `
    • ` — or on a `` *inside* an `

        `, where the single listener runs. Two properties do the work: - **`event.target`** — the deepest element actually clicked. Might be a child of the `
      • `, which is why you can't just use it directly. - **`.closest('li')`** — walks up from the target to the nearest matching ancestor, so a click on nested markup still resolves to the right row. The `list.contains(item)` guard matters when lists can nest: `closest` would happily find an `
      • ` above the `
          ` you're listening on. ## Why it's preferred **1. It works for elements that don't exist yet.** This is the real reason. Add a row after the listener is attached and it just works — no rebinding: ```javascript list.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '
        • Fourth

learnings.title: Critical Rendering Path & SPA Bootstrapping
learnings.source: user request: 1-day interview prep - browser & architecture
learnings.answer:
**The critical rendering path** is everything the browser does between receiving HTML bytes and painting the first pixel. Knowing it is what lets you answer *"what happens when you type a URL and press enter?"* — the most-asked browser question at this level.

To put it simply: the browser has to build two trees, combine them into a third, work out where everything goes, and only then can it paint.

## The full journey

**1. URL → IP.** DNS lookup, checked against the browser cache, OS cache, then a resolver.

**2. Connection.** TCP handshake, then a TLS handshake for HTTPS. Both cost round trips — which is why connection reuse and HTTP/2 matter.

**3. The HTML arrives** and the browser starts parsing *immediately*, as bytes stream in. It doesn't wait for the whole document.

**4. Two trees get built:**

- **DOM** — from the HTML
- **CSSOM** — from the CSS

**5. Render tree** — DOM and CSSOM combined, containing only what's actually visible. `display: none` nodes are excluded entirely. (`visibility: hidden` nodes *are* included — they occupy space.)

**6. Layout (reflow)** — compute the geometry of every box.

**7. Paint** — fill in pixels.

**8. Composite** — combine layers, potentially on the GPU.

Steps 6–8 are covered in more depth in [/css/6](/css/6).

## What actually blocks the render?

This is the part interviews probe, because it's where the practical decisions live.

**CSS is render-blocking.** The browser will not paint until the CSSOM is complete. It can't — it would risk showing unstyled content and then repainting everything. This is why `<link rel="stylesheet">` belongs in the `<head>` and why inlining critical CSS speeds up first paint.

**Synchronous JavaScript is parser-blocking.** When the parser hits `<script src>`, it stops building the DOM, fetches, executes, and only then resumes. Because a script might call `document.write`, the browser has no choice.

Worse: **a script also waits on any CSS above it**, because the script might read computed styles. So one stylesheet can delay a script which delays the DOM.

The two fixes:

```html
<script src="app.js" defer></script>  <!-- download in parallel, run after DOM is parsed, in order -->
<script src="a.js" async></script>    <!-- download in parallel, run the moment it lands, any order -->
```

**`defer` for application code** — order is preserved and the DOM exists when it runs. **`async` for independent third-party scripts** like analytics, where order doesn't matter.

## SPA bootstrapping — the part that's specific to your work

For a client-rendered React app, the sequence after the HTML arrives is:

1. HTML arrives — **essentially an empty `<div id="root">`**
2. The JS bundle downloads (often the biggest single cost)
3. The bundle parses and executes — *this is not free*; parsing a megabyte of JS is real CPU time, especially on a mid-range phone
4. React mounts and renders the initial tree
5. `useEffect` fires and the first data fetch **starts** — which means the user is now waiting on a *second* round trip that couldn't even begin until now
6. Data arrives, re-render, content appears

**That step-5 problem is the core weakness of client-side rendering**, and it's what SSR and server components address: with SSR the HTML already contains content, so the user sees something at step 1 instead of step 6.

With SSR you then have **hydration** — React walks the server-rendered HTML and attaches event listeners. Until hydration completes, the page *looks* ready but doesn't respond to clicks. That gap is a real UX problem and the reason streaming and selective hydration exist.

## The metrics they may name

| Metric | Means | Good |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **TTFB** | Time to first byte — server + network | < 800ms |
| **FCP** | First Contentful Paint — first content visible | < 1.8s |
| **LCP** | Largest Contentful Paint — main content visible | < 2.5s |
| **TTI** | Time to Interactive — actually responds to input | < 3.8s |
| **CLS** | Cumulative Layout Shift — visual stability | < 0.1 |
| **INP** | Interaction to Next Paint — replaced FID in 2024 | < 200ms |

**CLS** is the one with the most actionable fix: reserve space for images (`width`/`height` attributes or `aspect-ratio`) and for anything that loads late, so content doesn't jump.

## How to answer it out loud

> "DNS, TCP, TLS, then the HTML streams in and the parser starts building the DOM. CSS blocks rendering because you can't paint without the CSSOM, and synchronous scripts block the parser — so stylesheets go in the head and scripts get `defer`. DOM plus CSSOM gives the render tree, then layout, paint, composite.
>
> For an SPA there's an extra phase: the HTML is basically empty, so nothing shows until the bundle downloads, parses, and executes — and the first data fetch can't even start until React has mounted and effects run. That serial chain is why SSR helps, and why bundle size matters more than people expect on mobile."

## Trade-offs

- **Inlining critical CSS** speeds first paint but bloats the HTML and can't be cached separately.
- **Code splitting** reduces initial bundle size but adds round trips later — over-splitting produces a request waterfall ([/advanced-react/14](/advanced-react/14)).
- **SSR** improves perceived load but costs server compute and adds hydration complexity.
- **Preload/prefetch** (`<link rel="preload">`) can pull a critical resource forward, but over-preloading competes for bandwidth with the things that actually matter.

learnings.title: AJAX
Frontend API Architecture
learnings.source: user request: 1-day interview prep - browser & architecture
learnings.answer:
**Frontend API architecture** is the set of decisions about how your UI talks to the server: what shape the calls take, who owns error handling and retries, and where the boundary between client and server actually sits.

To put it simply: the question isn't "how do I call `fetch`" — it's "what layer owns the network, so that components don't have to."

## The Problem

`fetch` inside a component is fine exactly once. At scale it produces the same five problems in every codebase:

- The base URL and auth header are copy-pasted everywhere
- Error handling is inconsistent — some places catch, some don't
- Two components mounting together fire the same request twice
- Nothing is retried, or everything is retried including the things that shouldn't be
- Every component reimplements loading and error state

The fix is a **layer**, not a library. Even a thin one.

## The layers

```
Component        →  renders; knows nothing about HTTP
   ↓
Hook / query     →  caching, loading & error state, refetch
   ↓
API module       →  typed functions: getUsers(), createOrder()
   ↓
HTTP client      →  base URL, auth header, interceptors, retries
   ↓
Server / BFF
```

The rule that makes this work: **a component should never know a URL exists.** It calls `useUsers()`. If the endpoint moves, one file changes.

```javascript
// http.js — one place for cross-cutting concerns
async function request(path, options = {}) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE_URL}${path}`, {
    ...options,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...authHeader(), ...options.headers },
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    // Normalize failures into one error shape the whole app understands
    throw new ApiError(res.status, await res.json().catch(() => null));
  }

  return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json();
}

// api/users.js — the vocabulary of your domain, not of HTTP
export const getUsers = (params) => request(`/users?${new URLSearchParams(params)}`);
export const createUser = (body) => request('/users', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(body) });
```

**The `!res.ok` check is the detail interviewers look for.** `fetch` only rejects on *network* failure — a `404` or `500` resolves normally with `ok: false`. Code that only uses `.catch()` silently treats server errors as success. That's a real bug that ships often.

## REST vs GraphQL vs BFF

**REST** — resources and verbs. Simple, cacheable by HTTP out of the box, universally understood. Its weakness is shape: you get **over-fetching** (the endpoint returns 40 fields, you render 3) and **under-fetching** (you need three round trips to build one screen — the classic waterfall).

**GraphQL** — the client declares exactly what it needs, in one request. Solves both fetching problems and is excellent when many different clients need different shapes of the same data. Costs: HTTP caching no longer works out of the box (everything is a POST to one URL), you need query-complexity limits to prevent abuse, and the tooling is heavier. It also makes the N+1 problem the server's headache.

**BFF (Backend For Frontend)** — a thin server layer you own, sitting between your UI and the real services, shaping responses for exactly this frontend. The pragmatic middle ground: it kills over-fetching without adopting GraphQL, lets you keep secrets server-side, and gives you a same-origin API so CORS and cookie handling get simpler ([/browser/156](/browser/156)).

**How to answer "which would you pick?"** — Don't pick abstractly. *"Depends on how many clients consume this and how variable the data needs are. One web client against a stable API: REST, with a BFF if I'm fighting over-fetching. Several clients each needing different slices: GraphQL earns its complexity."*

## Errors, retries, and the details that matter

**Retry only what's safe.** `GET` is idempotent — retrying is harmless. Blindly retrying a `POST` can create two orders. Retry `GET`s and explicitly idempotent mutations; for the rest, use an idempotency key.

**Retry only what might succeed.** A `500` or a network blip, yes. A `400` or `422` will fail identically forever — retrying is pure latency.

**Back off exponentially**, with jitter. Fixed-interval retries from thousands of clients produce a thundering herd that keeps a recovering server down. You already have this at [/coding/25](/coding/25).

**Cancel what you don't need.** `AbortController` on unmount and on superseded requests:

```javascript
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  getUsers({ signal: controller.signal })
    .then(setUsers)
    .catch((err) => { if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err); });

  return () => controller.abort();
}, [query]);
```

**The race condition this prevents is the thing to name out loud.** Type "a", then "ab". Two requests in flight. If "a" resolves *second*, you render results for a query the user has moved past. Aborting — or the `cancelled` flag pattern — is what keeps the UI honest ([/advanced-react/15](/advanced-react/15)).

## Why you probably shouldn't hand-roll all of this

React Query / SWR / RTK Query give you caching, deduplication of in-flight requests, background refetch, retry with backoff, and cancellation — the things above, already correct.

**The framing that reads as senior:** server data is not really *state* you own. It's a **cache of something that lives elsewhere and changes without telling you.** Once you see it that way, putting it in Redux alongside your UI state feels wrong, and a purpose-built server-cache library feels obviously right ([/react-guide/27](/react-guide/27), [/react-learnings/26](/react-learnings/26)).

## Follow-ups

**"How do you handle a slow endpoint?"** — Diagnose first: slow server, large payload, or a waterfall? Fixes differ — pagination, field selection, parallelizing with `Promise.all`, prefetching on hover, or optimistic UI so the user isn't waiting at all.

**"Where does validation live?"** — Both ends. Client-side for fast feedback; server-side because the client can be bypassed entirely. Say both, always.

**"How do you handle partial failure on a dashboard?"** — `Promise.allSettled`, not `Promise.all`. One dead widget shouldn't blank the page. This is a great chance to show you know why `all`'s fail-fast is sometimes wrong ([/interview-prep/2](/interview-prep/2)).

**"Polling, SSE, or WebSockets?"** — Polling for infrequent updates, simplest and cache-friendly. **SSE** for one-way server push (notifications, live feeds) — plain HTTP, auto-reconnects. **WebSockets** when you need genuinely bidirectional, low-latency traffic (chat, collaborative editing), at the cost of connection state and scaling complexity.

learnings.title: HTTP Caching
learnings.source: user request: 1-day interview prep - browser & architecture
learnings.answer:
**HTTP caching** is how the browser avoids re-downloading things it already has. It's the cheapest performance win available, and the most common source of "why is the user still seeing the old version?"

To put it simply: the server attaches instructions to each response saying how long the browser may reuse it, and how to check cheaply whether it's still good.

## The Problem

Every asset re-downloaded is bandwidth, latency, and battery you didn't need to spend. But cache too aggressively and you ship a bug fix that nobody receives for a week. The whole subject is managing that tension.

## Two questions, two mechanisms

Caching answers two separate questions, and confusing them is where most bugs come from:

**1. "Can I skip the request entirely?"** → **freshness**, via `Cache-Control`.
**2. "It might be stale — has it actually changed?"** → **validation**, via `ETag` / `Last-Modified`.

The first avoids the network completely. The second still costs a round trip, but avoids re-downloading the body.

## `Cache-Control` — the directives that matter

```
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
```

| Directive | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `max-age=N` | Fresh for N seconds. **Don't even ask.** |
| `no-cache` | Cache it, but **revalidate every time** before use. Misleadingly named. |
| `no-store` | Never write it down at all. For sensitive data. |
| `private` | Browser may cache; shared caches and CDNs may not. |
| `public` | Any cache may store it, even with an `Authorization` header. |
| `immutable` | It will never change — skip revalidation even on reload. |
| `stale-while-revalidate=N` | Serve the stale copy instantly, refresh in the background. |

**`no-cache` does not mean "don't cache."** It means "cache, but always check first." `no-store` is the one that means don't cache. This distinction is a very common interview question precisely because the naming is bad.

## Validation — `ETag` and `304`

When something is stale but probably unchanged, the browser asks cheaply:

```
Response:  ETag: "abc123"
Later →    If-None-Match: "abc123"
Server  →  304 Not Modified          ← no body, just headers
```

A `304` is a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred kilobytes. `Last-Modified` / `If-Modified-Since` works the same way with a timestamp, but it's only second-granular and breaks when a rebuild changes mtimes without changing content. **`ETag` is the better mechanism.**

## The strategy that solves the tension

This is the answer to *"how do you cache aggressively without shipping stale code?"* — and it's what every modern bundler does:

**Content-hash your assets and cache them forever.**

```
/assets/app.a3f9c2.js     Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
/assets/main.7b21e4.css   Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
```

**Never cache the HTML.**

```
/index.html               Cache-Control: no-cache
```

The logic is elegant: the filename contains a hash of the contents, so **a changed file is a different URL**. There's no such thing as a stale `app.a3f9c2.js` — if the code changed, the name changed. Meanwhile `index.html` is revalidated on every visit, and it's the file that points at the new hashed names. One small conditional request unlocks the entire new build.

That's why Vite and webpack put hashes in output filenames by default. Being able to explain *why* is a strong answer.

## `stale-while-revalidate`

```
Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=3600
```

Fresh for 60 seconds. For the next hour, serve the **stale copy immediately** while fetching a fresh one in the background. The user never waits; the next visit gets the update.

The same idea drives React Query and SWR (the library is literally named after this header) at the application layer: show cached data instantly, refetch quietly, update when it lands.

## The layers of cache

A request can be answered at any of these, nearest first:

1. **Memory cache** — this tab, this session. Instant.
2. **Disk cache** — the browser's persistent HTTP cache.
3. **Service worker** — programmable; you control it in JS. Enables offline.
4. **CDN / edge** — shared across all users, near them geographically.
5. **Origin server** — and possibly its own Redis or application cache.

Use `private` to keep per-user responses out of layers 4 and 5. Getting that wrong means one user's data served to another — the worst caching bug there is, and worth naming as a risk.

## In application code

Beyond HTTP, the caching you actually write:

- **React Query / SWR** — the server-state cache: `staleTime`, `cacheTime`, background refetch, dedup of identical in-flight requests
- **`useMemo`** — caching a computed value across renders ([/react-guide/9](/react-guide/9))
- **Memoized functions** — caching by argument ([/coding/27](/coding/27))
- **`localStorage`** — persisting across sessions, but synchronous and easy to let go stale

## Trade-offs and follow-ups

**"How do you invalidate?"** — The honest answer is that you mostly don't. You make invalidation unnecessary by changing the URL (content hashing). Where you genuinely must invalidate, CDNs offer purge APIs, and cache tags let you purge a group.

**"What's the risk of caching too aggressively?"** — Users stuck on a broken build with no way to recover except a hard refresh. This is precisely why `index.html` is `no-cache` — it's the escape hatch that lets every other file be cached forever.

**"Should API responses be cached?"** — Depends on volatility and whether they're per-user. A public product list, absolutely — `max-age` plus `stale-while-revalidate`. A user's account page, `private, no-cache` at most. Anything with tokens or PII, `no-store`.

**"Service worker or HTTP cache?"** — HTTP caching first; it's declarative and hard to get catastrophically wrong. Service workers give you offline support and fine-grained control, at the cost of a genuinely tricky update lifecycle — a bad service worker can pin users to an old build semi-permanently.

learnings.title: CORS
learnings.source: user request: 1-day interview prep - browser & architecture
learnings.answer: **CORS** — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — is the mechanism by which a server tells the browser *"it's fine for this other origin to read my response."* To put it simply: CORS is not a wall that stops your request. It's a permission slip the server hands back, and the **browser** is the one enforcing it. ## The Problem it solves Without restrictions, any page you visit could fire a `fetch` at `your-bank.com`, ride along on your logged-in cookies, and read your balance. The **same-origin policy** exists to prevent that: by default, JavaScript on one origin cannot *read* responses from another. An **origin** is the triple `scheme + host + port`. All of these are cross-origin relative to `https://app.example.com`: | URL | Why | | --- | --- | | `http://app.example.com` | different scheme | | `https://api.example.com` | different host (a subdomain is a different host) | | `https://app.example.com:8080` | different port | But total lockdown is too strict — real apps legitimately call their own API on another domain. CORS is the controlled exception. ## What actually happens Here's the part that clears up most confusion: **the request usually goes through and the server usually processes it.** The browser then refuses to hand you the response because the right header wasn't on it. So a CORS error does not mean "blocked before sending." For a simple request, your backend already ran the code. This is why *a CORS failure can still have created a record in the database* — a genuinely surprising fact and a great thing to know. The browser sends an `Origin` header. The server must reply with: ``` Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com ``` If that header is absent or doesn't match, the browser discards the response and throws. Your `fetch` rejects; you cannot inspect the status or the body. ## Preflight — the `OPTIONS` request Some requests are considered **"simple"** and go straight out. A request is simple only if: - Method is `GET`, `HEAD`, or `POST`, **and** - The only headers set are a safe-listed few, **and** - `Content-Type` is one of `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data`, or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` Anything else — `PUT`, `DELETE`, a custom `Authorization` header, or (very commonly) **`Content-Type: application/json`** — triggers a **preflight**: the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request asking permission. ``` OPTIONS /api/users Origin: https://app.example.com Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization ``` The server must answer: ``` Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 ``` Only then does the real request go. **`Access-Control-Max-Age` caches that permission** so you're not paying an extra round trip on every call — a genuine performance detail worth raising. Note the asymmetry: a preflighted request that fails **never reaches your handler**. A simple request that fails **does**. ## Credentials — the trap everyone hits To send cookies cross-origin you need both sides to opt in: ```javascript fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }); ``` And the server must send: ``` Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com ← exact origin, NOT * Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true ``` **`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is rejected when credentials are involved.** The wildcard works fine until someone adds cookies, and then it breaks with an error message that doesn't obviously point at the wildcard. This is the single most common real-world CORS bug — knowing it in advance is worth a lot. ## The four failures you'll actually see 1. **"No `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header is present"** — the server isn't configured for CORS at all, or not for your origin. 2. **"The value of `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` must not be the wildcard when credentials mode is `include`"** — the wildcard-plus-cookies trap above. 3. **"Method PUT is not allowed by `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`"** — preflight rejected; the server didn't list your method. 4. **"Request header field `authorization` is not allowed"** — the server didn't list your custom header in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. ## How you fix it — in priority order **Configure the server.** This is the real fix. CORS is a *server* setting; there is no correct client-side workaround. **Use a dev proxy.** In Vite, `server.proxy` makes the request same-origin from the browser's point of view, so CORS never applies. Development only. **Same-origin in production via a reverse proxy or BFF** — serve the API under `/api` on the same origin. Then CORS is irrelevant *and* you can use `httpOnly` cookies without cross-site complications. **What is never the fix:** a browser extension that disables CORS, or `mode: 'no-cors'`. `no-cors` returns an **opaque** response — status 0, no readable body. It silences the error by making the response useless. Saying this explicitly is a good signal; a lot of people think `no-cors` is a solution. ## Follow-ups **"Why doesn't Postman get CORS errors?"** — Because CORS is enforced by *browsers*, not servers. Postman isn't a browser and has no origin to protect. This question is a direct test of whether you understand where enforcement lives. **"Why do `` and `

learnings.title: Cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage
learnings.source: user paste: senior frontend JS concepts
learnings.answer:
| Feature | Cookie | localStorage | sessionStorage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity | ~4KB (very small) | ~5MB–10MB | ~5MB |
| Expiration | Manually set (Expires/Max-Age) | Never (until deleted) | On tab/window close |
| Server Access | Sent with every HTTP request | Client-side only | Client-side only |
| Scope | Domain-wide | Domain-wide | Single tab/session |

## Cookies

Cookies are the oldest form of browser storage. Their primary purpose is **server-client communication**. Because they are sent to the server with every request, they are ideal for authentication tokens and session IDs.

- **Security:** Use `HttpOnly` to prevent JavaScript access (mitigating XSS) and `Secure` for HTTPS-only transmission.
- **Performance:** Large cookies slow down network performance since they're sent with every request.
- **Types:** **First-party cookies** are created by the site you're visiting; **third-party cookies** are set by other sites (e.g., advertisers).
- **Lifespan:** **Session cookies** are erased when you close the browser; **persistent cookies** remain until they expire or are deleted.

## `localStorage`

Introduced with HTML5, `localStorage` is a persistent key-value store for larger amounts of data that don't need to be sent to the server.

- **Persistence:** Data stays after the browser is closed. Removed only by user cache clear or explicit code.
- **Use case:** User preferences (Dark Mode), caching non-sensitive state, saving draft input.

## `sessionStorage`

Nearly identical API and capacity to `localStorage`, but lifecycle is much shorter.

- **Persistence:** Cleared when the specific tab or window closes.
- **Isolation:** Each tab has its own unique `sessionStorage` instance.
- **Use case:** Temporary data for a single session — multi-step wizards, one-time state that shouldn't leak to other tabs.

learnings.title: Auth & Security: JWT, XSS, CSRF
learnings.source: user request: 1-day interview prep - browser & architecture
learnings.answer: Authentication is **who you are**. Authorization is **what you're allowed to do**. Frontend interviews probe the first, and the storage decision that follows it. To put it simply: the server hands you proof of identity, and every subsequent request has to carry that proof. Where you put it is the whole security conversation. ## Two models **Session (stateful).** The server creates a session, stores it (in memory, Redis, a database), and sends you an opaque session ID in a cookie. Every request sends the cookie; the server looks it up. - Revoking is trivial — delete the session row and the user is out instantly - Requires server-side state, which needs sharing across instances **JWT (stateless).** The server signs a token containing claims (user id, roles, expiry). Nothing is stored server-side; the signature is what proves it wasn't tampered with. - Scales horizontally with no shared store — any instance can verify it - **Revoking is hard.** A valid token stays valid until it expires. If it's stolen, you cannot easily kill it A JWT is three base64 chunks: header, payload, signature. **The payload is signed, not encrypted** — anyone holding the token can decode and read it. Never put anything secret in a JWT. That's a favorite gotcha question. The standard mitigation for the revocation problem: **short-lived access tokens** (5–15 minutes) plus a **long-lived refresh token** stored more securely. The blast radius of a stolen access token is then minutes, not days. ## Where do you store the token? This is *the* frontend question, and the answer is a trade-off, not a rule. | | `localStorage` | `httpOnly` cookie | | --- | --- | --- | | Readable by JS | **Yes** — any XSS steals it | **No** — invisible to JS | | Sent automatically | No — you attach it | Yes — on every matching request | | Vulnerable to XSS | **Yes** | Much less | | Vulnerable to CSRF | No | **Yes** — needs `SameSite`/tokens | | Cross-domain API | Easy | Needs CORS credentials setup | **The strongest general answer:** > "I'd use an `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie for the refresh token, and keep the access token in memory only — a JS variable, not `localStorage`. Memory dies on refresh, so on load I silently exchange the refresh cookie for a fresh access token. > > That means an XSS can't read the refresh token at all, and the access token isn't sitting in persistent storage where a single injected script can scrape it. The cost is CSRF exposure on the refresh endpoint, which `SameSite` plus a CSRF token handles." That answer demonstrates you understand there's no free option — you're choosing which attack to defend against and mitigating the other. **Why `localStorage` is genuinely risky:** it is readable by *any* JavaScript running on the page. That includes every npm dependency and every third-party script. One compromised package and every token is exfiltrated. `httpOnly` cookies survive that scenario because JS simply cannot see them. ## XSS — Cross-Site Scripting **Attacker gets their JavaScript running on your page.** Then they have everything the user has. ```javascript // Attacker submits this as their display name: ``` **React protects you by default** — it escapes all interpolated values, so `{userInput}` renders as text, never as markup. The ways you lose that protection: - **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`** — the name is a deliberate warning. Sanitize with DOMPurify first. - **`href={userInput}`** — a `javascript:` URL executes on click. Validate the protocol. - **Rendering into the DOM manually** via a ref and `innerHTML`. - **`eval`** or `new Function` on anything user-derived. The defense in depth is **Content Security Policy** — a header restricting which script sources may execute: ``` Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' ``` With a strict CSP, even a successful injection often can't run, because inline scripts are blocked. ## CSRF — Cross-Site Request Forgery **The attacker doesn't steal your cookie — they get the browser to send it.** A hidden form on `evil.com` POSTs to `yourbank.com/transfer`, and the browser helpfully attaches your cookies because that's what cookies do. Note this only works against *automatic* credentials. It's a cookie problem specifically — a token you attach manually in an `Authorization` header isn't sent by a forged cross-site request. Defenses: - **`SameSite=Lax`** (the modern browser default) — cookies aren't sent on cross-site POSTs. This alone kills most CSRF. - **`SameSite=Strict`** — not sent on any cross-site request, including following a link *into* your site. More secure, worse UX. - **CSRF tokens** — a per-session random value the server requires in the body or a header. `evil.com` can't read it (same-origin policy), so it can't forge a valid request. **The clean one-liner:** *XSS steals the credential; CSRF abuses it in place. `httpOnly` stops the theft, `SameSite` stops the abuse.* ## The other things worth a sentence - **`Secure`** flag — cookie only over HTTPS. - **Clickjacking** — your site in an invisible iframe over a decoy. Fixed with `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or CSP `frame-ancestors`. - **Open redirect** — `?next=` pointing off-site. Validate redirect targets against an allowlist. - **Never trust the client.** Hiding an admin button is UX, not security. Every check must be re-done server-side. If they ask one authorization question, it's usually this. - **Secrets in the bundle** — anything in a frontend env var ships to the user. `VITE_`-prefixed variables are *public*. Only a backend may hold an API secret. ## OAuth in one paragraph You don't hand your password to a third party. You're redirected to the provider, you authorize, and they redirect back with a short-lived **code**, which your server exchanges for a token using its own secret. The code-plus-secret exchange is what stops an intercepted redirect from being useful. For public clients that can't hold a secret — SPAs and mobile apps — the modern requirement is **PKCE**, which substitutes a per-request generated verifier for the static secret. *OAuth is authorization; **OIDC** is the identity layer built on top that actually tells you who the user is.* ## Follow-ups **"How do you handle token expiry gracefully?"** — An interceptor: on a `401`, pause the failing request, refresh the token once, retry. Queue any concurrent requests so a burst of 401s doesn't trigger five parallel refreshes — that's the detail that shows you've built it. **"How do you log someone out everywhere?"** — Easy with sessions. With JWTs you need a revocation list or short expiry plus refresh-token invalidation — which is exactly the trade-off you accepted by going stateless. **"Is `localStorage` ever acceptable?"** — For a low-stakes internal tool, honestly yes, and pretending otherwise is dogma. But say what you're accepting: any XSS is a full account compromise.
